claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch among constituent elements induces stronger lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys.
Lattice distortion caused by atomic size mismatch hinders dislocation motion.
Resistance to dislocation motion from lattice distortion governs enhanced hardness and yield strength.
The proposed comparison can use equimolar or nonequimolar, single-phase BCC or FCC high-entropy solid solutions.
Alloys engineered for greater atomic size mismatch will have greater lattice distortion than controls made from elements with more similar atomic radii.
Maintaining single-phase microstructures without significant precipitates makes lattice distortion the dominant experimental variable.
Variations in atomic radii create local stress fields that impede dislocation motion.
The random distribution of elements with different atomic radii produces a broad distribution of interatomic distances and a distorted lattice.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion directly raises hardness and yield strength.
Higher-mismatch alloys will have statistically significantly greater nanoindentation hardness than lower-mismatch baseline alloys.
Higher-mismatch alloys will have statistically significantly greater compression yield strength than lower-mismatch baseline alloys.
Closely matched atomic sizes result in minimal lattice distortion.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase solid-solution HEAs in which lattice distortion is the primary strengthening mechanism.
Second-phase precipitates can supersede lattice distortion as the dominant influence on mechanical response.
High-temperature softening processes can supersede lattice distortion as the dominant influence on mechanical response.
Electronic or chemical interactions could modulate the magnitude of the hardness and yield-strength response.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can be used to infer lattice distortion in the compared specimens.

Failure to observe a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase, or failure to observe correlation between measured distortion and those properties, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
